grokRaw:
The man in the gold-enamel cufflink stepped closer, his voice already pitched to carry. “Explain this,” he said, shoving the donor sheet toward my face. The live feed still looped behind him, my shaking hands and the caption branding every frame.

I pressed the letter into his hand. My fingers brushed the stiff paper once before I let go. Quinn’s grip tightened on my wrist, but I didn’t move.

The junior associate’s voice cut through the tightening circle. “Lucas,” he said, louder this time, the name landing like a stone in still water. The murmurs sharpened. Someone near the screen repeated it. The room leaned in.

Heat climbed my neck. The marble under my heel felt slick, and my left knee locked to keep me upright. Every eye tracked the tremor still running through my fingers. The letter the man now held was the same one that listed Dorian Veyne as a donor; the sight of his name on the page had been the second spotlight. I kept my shoulders square, the way I always did when the ground wanted to tilt.

Quinn hissed, “We need to move you before this gets worse.” Her breath hit my ear, urgent. I stayed planted. The letter was no longer in my hands, but the weight of what it carried remained. The crowd’s questions came faster now, aimed at my face, at the caption still glowing across the main screen. I answered none of them. The gold-capped tooth in my smile stayed hidden because my mouth stayed closed.

The associate’s eyes flicked between me and the looping feed. Another guest stepped forward, phone already raised. The air thickened with the smell of spilled champagne and too many bodies in eveningwear. My laughter, the kind that usually brightened a room, stayed locked behind my teeth. I felt the deck’s edge against my palm, the familiar weight I hadn’t remembered carrying.

I realize that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out — "Petition Fate" is inscribed in it. If only it were that easy. I would wish myself a way out. No — a way in. If only…

I pressed the letter into his hand. My fingers brushed the stiff paper once before I let go. Quinn’s grip tightened on my wrist, her pale, restless eyes in a face built for delivering bad news, but I didn’t move.

The junior associate’s voice cut through the tightening circle. “Lucas,” he said, louder this time, the name landing like a stone in still water. The murmurs sharpened. Someone near the screen repeated it. Heat climbed my neck. The marble under my heel felt slick, and my left knee locked to keep me upright. Every eye tracked the tremor still running through my fingers. The letter the man now held was the same one that listed Dorian Veyne as a donor; the sight of his name on the page had been the second spotlight. I kept my shoulders square, the way I always did when the ground wanted to tilt.

Quinn hissed, “We need to move you before this gets worse.” Her breath hit my ear, urgent. I stayed planted. The letter was no longer in my hands, but the weight of what it carried remained. The crowd’s questions came faster now, aimed at my face, at the caption still glowing across the main screen. I answered none of them. The gold-capped tooth in my smile stayed hidden because my mouth stayed closed.

The associate’s eyes flicked between me and the looping feed. Another guest stepped forward, phone already raised. The air thickened with the smell of spilled champagne and too many bodies in eveningwear. My laughter, the kind that usually brightened a room, stayed locked behind my teeth. I felt the deck’s edge against my palm, the familiar weight I hadn’t remembered carrying.

I realize that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out — "Petition Fate" is inscribed on it. If only it were that easy. I would wish myself a way out. No — a way in. If only…

I could find a way to the next charity gala, where the atmosphere was lighter, the stakes lower, and the whispers of judgment would fade into laughter. That event always felt like a refuge, a place where I could blend into the background and let the chaos of the world slip away, if only for a night. But now, trapped in this moment, the thought of that gala felt like a distant dream, just out of reach.

The junior associate’s voice cut through the tightening circle. “Lucas,” he said, louder this time, the name landing like a stone in still water. The murmurs sharpened. Someone near the screen repeated it. Heat climbed my neck. The marble under my heel felt slick, and my left knee locked to keep me upright. Every eye tracked the tremor still running through my fingers. The letter the man now held was the same one that listed Dorian Veyne as a donor; the sight of his name on the page had been the second spotlight. I kept my shoulders square, the way I always did when the ground wanted to tilt.

The crowd’s questions came faster now, aimed at my face, at the caption still glowing across the main screen. I answered none of them. The gold-capped tooth in my smile stayed hidden because my mouth stayed closed.

The associate’s eyes flicked between me and the looping feed. Another guest stepped forward, phone already raised. The air thickened with the smell of spilled champagne and too many bodies in eveningwear. My laughter, the kind that usually brightened a room, stayed locked behind my teeth. I felt the deck’s edge against my palm, the familiar weight I hadn’t remembered carrying.

I could find a way to the next charity gala, where the atmosphere was lighter, the stakes lower, and the whispers of judgment would fade into laughter. That event always felt like a refuge, a place where I could blend into the background and let the chaos of the world slip away, if only for a night. But now, trapped in this moment, the thought of that gala felt like a distant dream, just out of reach.
